idiom_name: EventEmitter<DomainEventMap> from node:events with typed payload tuples
implementation_notes: TypeScript's practical default is the platform dispatcher typed by a map: declare interface DomainEvents { 'order.placed': [OrderPlaced] } and class OrderBus extends EventEmitter<DomainEvents>, so emit checks the payload tuple and on infers the listener parameter. The runtime is Node's EventEmitter (the generic signature comes from @types/node; Bun and Deno expose the same API), and the event objects remain hand-written interfaces or classes named in the past tense. Names are still strings at runtime, so the type map is the only thing keeping them honest.
pitfalls: emit does not validate the payload at runtime: data crossing a process boundary must be re-validated before it is trusted as an event.

Listeners are synchronous and exceptions propagate out of emit, so one failing subscriber aborts the rest and can fail the publishing operation; choose captureRejections or an async policy deliberately.

variants.name: Kind-tagged discriminated union + typed publish/subscribe bus
variants.implementation_notes: When events should be values the whole application speaks (log, persist, replay), model them as one discriminated union with a kind literal and derive the bus from it: EventOf<K> extracts the matching variant, publish<K>(kind, event) makes a mismatched payload a compile error, and catch-all switches end with assertNever so adding a variant breaks every exhaustive handler. The bus itself is a Map of handler sets - the classic registry with the type system checking the routing; it also works in browsers where node:events is absent.
pitfalls: A catch-all subscriber that switches over the union and omits the assertNever default silently ignores future event kinds.
Union members are structural: a missing or renamed kind literal is caught only where the value is typed as DomainEvent, so construct events through typed factory functions.
